newsitem.title: USA: Scientists to map all human genes by 2005.
newsitem.headline: Scientists to map all human genes by 2005.

text.p: By 2005, scientists expect to have analysed all three billion human DNA sequences responsible for everything from hair colour to the ability to fight off disease, a researcher said on Wednesday.

So far, using a painstaking and expensive process, scientists have mapped just 2 percent of known genetic sequences, Robert Waterston, director of the Genome Sequencing Centre at Washington University in St. Louis, Mo., said.
The lab is one of about a dozen worldwide that are collaborating on the project, including centres in the United States, Germany, Japan and England.
The scientists, who started the project in 1995, hope their work will aid in the understanding and treatment of disease, Waterston told a Harvard University symposium on genetic research in Boston.
The work of the Human Genome Project has helped scientists find genes linked to breast and colon cancer, cystic fibrosis, Alzheimer's disease and obesity.
"Mapping the genes is like building highways and roads. It is infrastructure," Waterston said.

The laboratories involved in the project have agreed to forego patenting their discoveries and instead place all the information on an Internet website for public use. Other scientists and biotechnology companies can use the information to research disease and develop treatments.
"We want the information out there for everyone to use," Waterston said.
